video_title: How a 21-Year-Old Conquered the Unbreakable City: Constantinople (1453)

acts.title: What This Story Is About: The Unbreakable City
acts.script: This is the story of how a twenty-one-year-old ruler named Sultan Mehmed captured Constantinople, the most unbreakable city on Earth, in just fifty-three days. For over a thousand years, twenty-three different armies had tried to take this city and failed. To finally break it, Mehmed had to do something nobody had ever seen: sail seventy warships across dry land. Why was Constantinople so hard to capture? Because the city sat on a triangle of land surrounded by deep water on two sides, and the only land entrance was blocked by three giant stone walls. Because plagues and past wars had shrunk the Roman Empire down to this one last city, Emperor Constantine had only seven thousand soldiers left to defend the walls against eighty thousand Ottoman troops.

acts.title: Because Catapults Failed: The 27-Foot Monster Cannon
acts.script: Even with only seven thousand men, the defenders felt safe because no catapult in history could break their forty-foot walls. So Sultan Mehmed hired an engineer named Urban to build a twenty-seven-foot bronze monster cannon. When this giant cannon fired, the explosion shook the ground for two miles, and its twelve-hundred-pound stone ball smashed huge sections of the ancient wall into dust. But the giant cannon had a huge problem: the bronze barrel got so hot that it took three hours to cool down and reload. Because it could only fire seven times a day, the city's citizens ran out every night with barrels of dirt and wood to plug the holes before morning.

acts.title: Because the Harbor Was Blocked: Sailing 70 Ships Across a Mountain
acts.script: Because attacking the thick land walls wasn't working, Mehmed realized he needed to attack the northern harbor, where the city wall was thin and weak. But the defenders had stretched a giant floating iron chain across the harbor entrance, blocking every Ottoman ship from sailing in. Because his ships couldn't go through the iron chain, Mehmed decided to go around it across dry land. On the night of April twenty-first, thousands of workers built a two-mile road of wooden logs over the steep hill behind the chain and greased the wood with animal fat. Using teams of oxen and hundreds of soldiers pulling ropes, they dragged seventy warships up and over the hill in a single night. When the defenders woke up the next morning, they were horrified to see an entire enemy fleet floating inside their safe harbor. Because the harbor wall was now in danger, the Emperor was forced to pull soldiers away from the main land walls to guard the water. His tiny army was now stretched to the breaking point.

acts.title: The Final Twist: One Unlocked Door Ends a 1,500-Year Empire
acts.script: By Day fifty-three, on May twenty-ninth, Mehmed knew the defenders were exhausted and out of supplies. Before sunrise, he ordered an all-out attack against both the land walls and the harbor at the exact same time. For two hours, the defenders fought bravely and pushed back two huge waves of attackers. But in the chaos, a retreating group of soldiers made one fatal mistake: they forgot to lock a tiny side door in the wall called the Kerkoporta. Fifty Ottoman soldiers spotted the unlocked door, rushed inside, climbed to the top of the tower, and raised the Ottoman flag. When the defenders fighting below looked up and saw the enemy flag flying above them, they panicked and shouted that the city had fallen. Seeing the line collapse, Emperor Constantine tore off his royal purple cape so nobody would recognize him, charged into the battle like an ordinary soldier, and was never seen alive again. By noon, Sultan Mehmed rode through the gates into the city. Because Constantinople had fallen, the fifteen-hundred-year-old Roman Empire ended forever, the trade routes to Asia were closed, and European explorers were forced to sail west across the Atlantic—leading directly to the discovery of the Americas.
